genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a food warehouse
the winter deliveries kept arriving incomplete
the shops she supplied ran short of goods
she blamed the hauliers and the suppliers first
she realized the mess came from her own building
the heavy goods were moved close to the doors
painted lanes on the floor now organize the movement
the handlers laughed at the change at first
the crews walk shorter distances
not one order went short the following season
text: The woman who ran the food warehouse knew the smell of damp cardboard better than anyone. Every winter brought the same ordeal back to her door. The trucks pulled in half empty, and the shops she was meant to supply cleared their shelves faster than she could fill them. She blamed the hauliers first, then the suppliers, before admitting that the mess started inside her own building. So she sat down and rethought the whole place. Heavy stock went by the doors, rare items to the back, and she painted colored lanes across the floor that nobody crossed without a reason. The handlers laughed at her, then came around, because their walking shrank. The next season, not one order went short. She tells it without pride, the way you describe something obvious that took you several winters to see.

units: two assembly shops are set against each other
the first put its money into one costly machine
that machine cuts and folds with no operator
the second shop lines up three modest stations set by hand
the integrated line runs faster than the three stations
the single machine takes many seasons to pay for itself
one breakdown of the single machine halts all production
the modest stations are mended with ordinary parts
the integrated setup pays off when demand stays steady and high
the writer concludes that the choice depends on the customers
text: Setting the two assembly shops side by side means weighing two ways of putting money to work. The first backed one costly machine that cuts and folds with nobody standing over it. The second chose three modest stations, set by hand, watched in turn by a single worker. On paper the integrated line wins. It runs faster than the three stations together, and the man on the floor merely confirms the settings. Watching the shops work softens that verdict. The one machine takes many seasons to pay for itself, and a single breakdown freezes everything behind it. The three stations rarely fail together, and ordinary parts put them back to work. The integrated shop pays off as soon as demand holds steady and high. The split shop takes ragged orders better. What decides the matter is who buys from you, not the spec sheet.

units: the writer answers a request for advice in writing
the reader is starting out in the same trade
he urges reading contracts down to the termination clauses
a shaky engagement shows itself in its annexes
he advises checking that the employer really pays the contributions
he recommends keeping your pay slips
he warns against rushing the pay talk out of embarrassment
a wage set badly at the outset weighs on you for a long time
he urges keeping company with others in the trade to hear about bad employers
the writer offers his help if trouble comes
text: You asked what I would tell someone just starting out in our trade, and I am glad to answer in writing, so that nothing of it gets lost. First of all, contracts. Read them through to the termination clauses, because a shaky engagement shows itself in the annexes rather than in the title. Second, social cover. Make certain your employer really pays in the contributions owed on your behalf, ask for your pay slips, and file them away. Third, money. Never rush a pay talk out of embarrassment, since a figure set badly at the outset will weigh on you for a long time. Fourth, company. Keep company with others who do the same work, and they will tell you which houses to steer clear of. Last of all, spare your own strength. I wish you a calm beginning, and my help is yours should trouble come.

units: an employment adviser answers a run of questions
she puts the starting point in taking stock of your own skills
the second stage is spotting employers who hire without saying so
then come applications shaped to each place
she warns that many refusals are to be expected
discouragement often arrives before the first interview
she advises writing down every step taken in a notebook
keeping that notebook turns waiting into actions you can measure
she advises preparing the interview by studying what the firm does
she warns against mistaking slow hiring for unfairness
text: Where does a job search begin? The adviser brushes the expected answer aside. You do not begin by writing, you begin by taking honest stock of what you can actually do. And then? Then comes the stage of spotting the employers who are hiring without having said so yet. After that you approach them, one letter at a time, shaping each one to the place it goes to. How many refusals lie ahead? More than you picture, she grants, and the weariness usually sets in before the first interview. What holds a person together? A notebook, with every step written into it, which turns waiting into a run of actions you can measure. And the interview itself? You prepare for it by studying what the firm does, instead of reciting your own past. Her closing word is short. Hiring is slow, and slow is not the same as unfair.

units: a neighbor tells the narrator about his picking season
he had been taken on for the length of the harvest
his pay hung on the number of crates he filled
the crop came in heavy right across the region
the buyers forced the price down to half the usual one
the growers sold cheap rather than let the fruit rot
the rate paid per crate fell
the pickers took home less for gathering more
he means to go back next season
he will insist on a rate written down before he leaves
text: Back from the picking season, the neighbor downstairs held nothing back. He had been taken on for the harvest, paid by the crate, in an orchard where the work ran from first light until dark. The crop came in heavy right across the region, he told me, so the buyers set the terms. They offered half the usual price, and the growers let it go cheap rather than watch the fruit rot on the branch. The rate per crate dropped, and the pickers took home less for gathering more. He shrugged his shoulders at that. When an orchard overflows, he said, nobody comes out ahead, not even the man doing the selling. He means to go back all the same, since he knows the ground and knows where to sleep for nothing. But he will not leave again, he told me, without a rate written down and signed beforehand.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before common funds one accident ruined a craftsman's family
the workshop hung on the bodily strength of a single person
archives tell of widows forced to sell the tools
apprentices were sent back to the countryside they came from
the answer came from the workshops themselves with no help from those in power
every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals
the fund replaced a ruined tool and kept an injured man fed
it also paid for the burial of a master craftsman
historians stress how slowly the idea took hold
the arrangement was later taken over by the public authorities
text: Before the trades built up common funds, one accident was enough to ruin a craftsman's family. The danger was plain to everybody. A workshop hung on a single pair of hands, and hands got broken. The old trade archives tell of widows who had to sell the tools in order to eat, and of apprentices sent back to the countryside they came from. The answer grew out of the workshops themselves, with no help from anyone in power. Every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals. The fund replaced a ruined tool, kept an injured man fed, and paid for a master's burial. What strikes historians is how slowly the thing was invented. Whole generations passed before people would accept that a risk falling on one man is easier to carry among many. Once accepted, it spread fast, and the public authorities took it over much later.

units: a fixed wage is likened to a running stream
the earnings of a self-employed worker are likened to rainfall
the wage earner can plan his spending because the money comes in evenly
the self-employed worker knows fat stretches and empty ones
the difference lies in the evenness and not in the amount
on the same yearly earnings the self-employed worker is lent money less readily
the lender is after evenness rather than wealth
the self-employed worker has to make that evenness himself
he does it by holding back what the fat seasons leave him
text: A wage is a stream. What a worker earns on his own account is rainfall. The stream carries no more water than the rain does, yet it keeps running. Whoever draws steady pay can plan what to spend, sign a lease, promise to pay a sum back, because he knows in advance how much will pass under his feet. Whoever lives off showers goes through fat weeks and then dry ones. The money pours down, then nothing falls at all. So the difference lies in the shape and not in the sum. That is what lights up a fact that looks strange at first. On the same yearly earnings, the second is lent money far less readily than the first. A lender is not buying wealth, what he is buying is evenness. And whoever lives on rain has to make that evenness himself, by holding back whatever the fat seasons leave behind.

units: a routine inspection was aimed at a packaging plant
the inspector wrote up faults of four different kinds
pallets of resin were stored too close to the ovens
that heat explained why some batches came out warped
the dosing unit had gone far too long without calibration
the setters corrected its drift by hand and wrote nothing down
half the night crew lacked the certificate the post called for
the scrapped parts appeared in no accounting record
the head of the site blamed the pressure of the orders
the inspector puts these faults down to checking let slide again and again
text: It was supposed to be nothing more than a routine call at a packaging plant, and the inspector came away with faults of four kinds. Take the materials first. The pallets of resin sat close enough to the ovens to pass the heat limit, which explained the warped batches. Machines next. The dosing unit had gone far too long without calibration, and the setters had been correcting its drift by hand, writing nothing down. Staffing after that. Half of the night crew held posts they had no certificate for at all. Records last. The scrapped parts turned up in none of the production accounts. The head of the site pleaded the pressure the orders were putting on him. The inspector answered that nothing she had just written up came from haste. It came from checking let slide, season after season.

units: the procedure covers the opening of a retail shop
the steps must not be swapped around
the first is to gauge what the neighborhood wants
that gauging is done by watching the passers-by and the storefronts nearby
the business must be registered before any goods are ordered
the lease has to carry an exit clause
the first range of goods is kept narrow on purpose to spare the cash
a trial week with no advertising serves to adjust the prices
a record of what comes in and goes out is kept from the first sale on
text: Work through these steps in the order they are given here, because opening a retail shop allows no swapping around. Begin by gauging what the neighborhood wants. Count the people going past, note the storefronts already there, ask those who live nearby. Register the business next with the office appointed for it, since no goods may be ordered before that formality is done. Negotiate the lease after that, and insist on an exit clause, because a badly chosen space is harder to leave than to take. Put together your first range of goods, narrow on purpose. Better to run out of an article than to tie up your cash. Open the doors quietly for a trial week, with no advertising, so that prices and hours can be adjusted. Keep a record of what comes in and goes out, from the first sale on.

units: the closing of a cannery has been announced
the plant used to buy the catch of the fleet nearby
the skippers put to sea less and sell straight to customers at a loss
the boatyards have cut their staff
the shops on the main street are seeing fewer customers
the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally
elected officials are calling for an investor to take the site over
nobody has come forward because rebuilding the cold chain costs too much
an association of workers proposes buying the plant together
the outgoing management has not answered that proposal
text: Since the cannery announced it would close, the working district around it has taken one blow after another. The plant used to buy the catch from the fleet nearby. With that outlet gone, the skippers put to sea less often and sell straight to customers, at a loss. The boatyards that lived off their orders have cut staff in turn. The shops on the main street already count fewer customers through the door, because the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally. Elected officials are calling for an investor to take the site over, yet nobody has come forward, since rebuilding the cold chain would cost too much. An association of workers is pushing another way out: buying the plant together and turning it to small runs of goods. The outgoing management has said nothing so far.
